https://www.delfi.lt/en/politics/preside.text: Delfi EN Delfi Politics 2026.07.22 10:15 President’s adviser hopes for closer economic cooperation with Taiwan Source: ELTA Deividas Matulionis PHOTO: Audrius Gavėnas | Elta Follow Delfi on Google Although the new Social Democratic Government’s programme no longer mentions relations with Taiwan, yet President’s Chief National Security Adviser Deividas Matulionis vows that Lithuania will continue striving to develop pragmatic economic cooperation with the island in East Asia. Nonetheless, he adds that Lithuania expected a greater economic benefit from cooperating with Taiwan. „In the [Government’s] programme we do set certain priorities, perhaps there is less focus [on Taiwan], but everything depends on Taiwan itself, whether they are indeed willing to step up economic cooperation. So far, there has been little visible practical economic benefit, while we would certainly like to see more of it,“ Matulionis said in an interview to the radio station Žinių radijas on Tuesday. The adviser to President Gitanas Nausėda emphasised that „nothing has changed regarding Taiwan“. „The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is very actively harmonising the so-called action plan on economic cooperation. We continue to be interested in pragmatic economic cooperation, whether these are investments, or trade, or innovations. Whether there is such a sentence in the Government’s programme or not, it does not change anything,“ said the adviser. He added that Lithuania has two goals – to restore diplomatic ties with China and, at the same time, to develop economic ties with Taiwan. „Relations with Taiwan are pragmatic relations. They are important to us. We want investments, we want cooperation in the area of development of semiconductors and in the area of innovation because Taiwan is the world leader in this regard,“ said the president’s adviser. As reported, the Lithuanian Parliament recently approved the programme of the 21st Government led by Social Democratic Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius and the new Cabinet of Ministers was sworn in. Lithuania’s relationships with China deteriorated when the Taiwanese Representative Office was opened in Vilnius in November 2021. China, which regards Taiwan to be its breakaway province, has objected to using the name of Taiwan rather than Taipei. In retaliation, Beijing imposed tough diplomatic and economic sanctions. China downgraded the level of its diplomatic representation in Lithuania. In February 2022, Lithuania appealed to the European Commission and lodged a complaint against China at the World Trade Organisation (WTO). The EU stated that Beijing applied discriminatory practices against Lithuania as trade restrictions, ostensibly imposed due to hygiene issues, cut Lithuania’s exports to China by 80% that year. In December 2025, the EU withdrew its complaint at the WTO. Beijing previously stated that doors were open for bilateral cooperation, but Vilnius had to „correct the error“ regarding the Taiwanese Representative Office. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes. Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/AP View image in fullscreen Asháninka Indigenous people dance and sing during an annual celebration recognising the Asháninka territory. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes. Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/AP Indigenous peoples People protecting nature and land set up self-defence units amid threat of murder Defenders of forests and rivers killed at rate of one every three days in 2025, with 85% of deaths in Latin America Jonathan Watts Wed 16 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 01.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last year, prompting many communities to set up self-defence units, according to the latest annual death toll by the independent watchdog Global Witness. Organised crime groups or professional killers were implicated in more than a third of the 124 killings of defenders in 2025 as narco-trafficking activities overlapped with intrusions into indigenous territories and environmental crime, such as illegal logging and wildcat gold mining. This was particularly true in Latin America, which accounted for 85% of last year’s deaths of people trying to protect forests, rivers and other ecosystems. Colombia had the highest toll with 39 killings, followed by Brazil with 26 and Honduras with 12. In Asia, the most dangerous country for defenders was the Philippines , with 12 killings – many during crackdowns by state security forces. View image in fullscreen Asháninka territory in Brazil sits along the winding Amônia River. Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community. Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/AP Since Global Witness began compiling statistics in 2012, the overall global tally is now 2,375 deaths and disappearances – on a par with a small-scale war. On a more positive note, the headline figure has declined over the last two years, from 196 in 2023 and 142 in 2024, though the report authors say this is likely to be an underestimate because data collection is difficult in war zones and authoritarian regimes. Many countries and companies are also carrying out nonlethal attacks on defenders, including criminalisation and online smear campaigns. Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community, partly as a result of cuts by the Trump administration. “The dismantling of USAID, which previously supported initiatives for Indigenous peoples to steward their own land, has had particularly serious implications for defenders,” the report says. Almost three-quarters of the killings documented in 2025 were of Indigenous people and small-scale farmers targeted for defending their land. With less outside help, an increasing number of these communities are establishing their own territorial defence mechanisms. The report highlights the example of the Kakataibo Indigenous Guard in the Peruvian Amazon. Six of the community’s leaders have been killed since 2020 amid growing incursions into the forest by criminal groups. Starting in 2022 with a few dozen recruits, the guard now has more than 150 volunteers in its 10 bases. Segundo Ispón, the commander of the organisation, said the self-defence groups provided a global benefit: “Defending our territory is important to us as a community and as a people, and we’re proud to support the climate that we all depend on. In our culture, the work of defending our resources and territory is taught from an early age. But for this next generation coming up, the work is more dangerous than ever.” At least a dozen other communities in Peru have organised self-defence units. Similar bodies have existed for some years in Colombia and Brazil. But it is risky. Last year, seven Indigenous guards were murdered. In at least five of these cases, the killings were linked to organised crime. Many forest communities report the narco-threat is growing closer. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes, apparently in search of assassination targets. In the Ucayali basin on the other side of the border, Global Witness said there was a 600% increase in coca production between 2019 and 2023. This is pushing gangs to expand smuggling networks, including through the opening of illegal roads and trails through the forest. Corruption further adds to the risks facing forest protectors who stand in their way because many local politicians and police are in the pay of the traffickers. View image in fullscreen An Indigenous person looks out over Apurímac River valley in Peru. Local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists have been threatened after calling for a more effective state presence across affected countries. Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty Images Forest communities want help from governments to ease these pressures but there are concerns the opposite may be happening. Under US leadership, many rightwing governments are pursuing military crackdowns on coca growers and drug traffickers, which is pushing narco-gangs further into remote regions and indigenous territories. Ricardo Soberón, a former head of Peru’s anti-narcotics office, said many communities were also affected on the border of Peru and Colombia. “We are in a situation where transnational criminal groups have appropriated the daily life of the Huitoto, Quichua, Bora, Secoya Indigenous people, who live along the Putumayo basin,” he said. Of particular concern, he added, were the threats against local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists who call for a more effective state presence. He fears the newly elected rightwing governments in affected countries will make matters worse by militarising the conflict in line with the “America shield” priorities of the Trump administration. Global Witness has urged the authorities to respect and work with nature and land defenders rather than making their role more difficult. Toby Hill, the lead author of the report, said: “Defenders are the world’s eyes and ears on the ground. It’s thanks to them that we know when ecosystems are being destroyed, where forests are being cleared or rivers polluted. We can’t forget the thousands of defenders around the world who are working every day to protect their territories and cultures under increasing pressure.” Explore more on these topics Indigenous peoples Peru Brazil Organised crime Americas Amazon rainforest Drugs trade news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text: World of knowledge … Gösta Ekman as Faust. Photograph: Courtesy of Mubi View image in fullscreen World of knowledge … Gösta Ekman as Faust. Photograph: Courtesy of Mubi Movies Review Faust review – FW Murnau’s silent masterpiece is a devilishly dazzling vision The 1926 film of Goethe’s tragic tale of a man who sells his soul to the devil remains a spectacular feat of German expressionism Peter Bradshaw Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he centenary of FW Murnau’s silent fantasy-melodrama from 1926 is the occasion to ponder this mysterious film, taken from Goethe’s 19th-century depiction of the alchemist and natural philosopher who sells his soul to the devil but, in a very high-minded climax of German romanticism, is redeemed by love. (Not love of God precisely, but love of a good woman; the word “Liebe” finally appears at the centre of Murnau’s radiating vision of concentric circles conjured by the heavens, which annul his debt to the Evil One.) It is therefore very different from Christopher Marlowe’s scarier and more unforgiving account of Doctor Faustus. Murnau’s Faust is (obviously) concerned with and animated by evil, and there are echoes of his Nosferatu , made four years previously. In this film, Faust, having struck his bargain on a provisional 24-hour basis with Mephisto, finds that he is scared of a crucifix, like a vampire. It is also very much a film of Weimar Germany with its mad energy and streaks of garish satire and black comedy; the book-burning scene in which Faust immolates all his necromancy volumes, along with the Bible, is one which resonated with later events. (Perhaps it indirectly inspired Klaus Mann’s novel Mephisto, later to be filmed by István Szabó .) Gösta Ekman plays Faust, ancient and grey-haired like an Old Testament prophet (or like God himself), and the veteran stager Emil Jannings (who, two years later, made Hollywood history by winning the first best actor Oscar) is the grinning, gurning Mephisto who makes a celestial wager that he can corrupt a decent man. This, of course, is Faust, who is wretched at the plague and devastation everywhere about and despairingly throws his learned books in the fire, but is then captivated by a charred page which tells of how to sell your soul at a distant crossroads. (Did this start the tradition carried on by bluesman Robert Johnson, who reputedly did something similar?) Mephisto offers him whatever he wants, including a “bacchanal” or orgy, and gives him an opportunity to dally with the Duchess of Parma, “the most beautiful woman in Italy”. But Faust ultimately wants to go back to his home village as the young man he once was, and there falls in love with comely innocent Gretchen (Camilla Horn), while Mephisto, that capering lord of misrule, has knockabout high-jinks with Gretchen’s blowsy Aunt Marthe (Yvette Guilbert). It is to lead to horror, with Gretchen sentenced to be burned at the stake for murdering the child she conceived with Faust, who is in turn wanted for killing Gretchen’s outraged brother Valentin (William Dieterle, himself to become an Oscar-winning Hollywood director) in a duel. The ambition, scale and drive of Faust are obvious: there is some wonderful model work for the landscape and cityscape that Faust and Mephisto look down on, flying above. And the still, painterly image of Mephisto as a vast evil angel, brooding over the city like a gigantic cloud, shrouding it in his black wings, is inspired. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: The Guardian uncovered a series of cases showing how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts. Photograph: Kathy images/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen The Guardian uncovered a series of cases showing how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts. Photograph: Kathy images/Shutterstock Base justice UK news UK police should not have let US force take over airbase trial, MoD documents show According to documents obtained by the Guardian, officials accused Cambridgeshire force of breaching US-UK deal by handing over case of woman strangled by US pilot Rob Evans , Harry Davies , Louisa Loveluck and Emine Sinmaz Sat 31 Oct 2026 09.30 EDT Last modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 09.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ministry of Defence officials have privately accused a UK police force of wrongly handing over the investigation of an American fighter pilot who strangled a British woman to the US military, according to documents obtained by the Guardian. Cambridgeshire police allowed the US military police to quickly take control of the investigation into Capt Jacob Wulfson after he had been accused of sexually assaulting Sarah Steele in his Cambridge flat. The decision meant Wulfson was not tried in an English criminal court. Instead he was prosecuted in a military tribunal on a US airbase in neighbouring Suffolk. View image in fullscreen An all-male jury of Capt Jacob Wulfson’s fellow air force officers convicted him of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted him of sexual assault. Photograph: United States Air Forces Central Ministry of Defence officials said the Cambridgeshire force should “absolutely” not have let the US military police take over the investigation in a clear breach of a long-established agreement with the US. The disclosure of the case by the Guardian in June provoked immediate criticism from Downing Street , which said it was “deeply distressing” and “very concerning” that the UK authorities were not involved in prosecuting Wulfson. ‘Degrading’: why did a US fighter pilot avoid British trial after strangling a woman in England? Read more The government to set up a high-level inquiry to examine how and why police forces have been transferring investigations into serious crimes to the US military police. The Ministry of Defence, which is responsible for handling the military relationship with the US, is one of the key departments taking part in the inquiry. A batch of documents, disclosed via the Freedom of Information Act, revealed the private views of MoD officials about the Steele case, which centres on an obscure agreement signed by the US and the UK decades ago. Under the terms of the agreement, police in the UK have the primary right to investigate alleged crimes by Americans stationed in the country . The MoD officials made it clear the agreement was “pretty unambiguous” and only permitted the US military to acquire jurisdiction over investigations in a “narrow set of circumstances”. These circumstances are: if the offences were committed while the Americans were on duty, or if they were committed against another member of their armed forces or property. In a memo written on 8 July, MoD officials based in Washington wrote: “The Steele case does not, on the surface, appear to meet the bar for a visiting force to be awarded jurisdiction.” In the agreement, the US military is formally known as a visiting force. Four days earlier, the MoD officials had referred to the Steele case in an email to colleagues, saying: “The decision-making on this specific case seemed at odds with what is very clear” in the agreement. Another MoD official agreed that “as best as we understand the facts, this should absolutely have been for the UK courts”. An unidentified Greater Manchester police officer wrote in an email to MoD officials on 6 July that Cambridgeshire police had “wrongly, in my view” handed over the Wulfson investigation to the US military. Cambridgeshire police said they were conducting a review of the case with what they called “the assistance of material provided” by US Air Force lawyers. The force said it “remained engaged with the victim”. “We are working with government, wider policing and criminal justice partners to ensure greater clarity of jurisdictional decision making,” they added. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion How the US bypasses British courts to try its military over crimes in the UK Read more The US military aims to prosecute as many of its personnel as possible within the boundaries of its agreement with the UK. The Americans often ask police in the UK if they can take over the prosecution of their military personnel – requests the police agree to, even when they have primary responsibility for investigating them. A series of cases uncovered this year by the Guardian have highlighted concerns that British victims are required to give evidence in US courts martial, an unfamiliar legal system that often does not afford the same protections as that of a court in the UK. Wulfson was off-duty when he assaulted Steele in his Cambridge flat in December 2023 after the pair talked on the Tinder dating app. Steele testified at Wulfson’s court martial, which was held on his airbase at Lakenheath, Suffolk in April, that her experience was “degrading and distressing” . The verdict and sentence were decided by an all-male jury of Wulfson’s fellow air force officers. All the lawyers were American. Steele was subjected to invasive and aggressive questioning by Wulfson’s lawyer. Wulfson was convicted of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted of sexual assault. He was dismissed from the US Air Force and confined to a military jail on Lakenheath for six months. The cross-government inquiry, which includes officials from the Home Office, Ministry of Justice and Foreign Office, is looking at how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts. The inquiry, which also involves police chiefs, is scrutinising a series of cases uncovered by the Guardian this year. In each case, police handed over the investigations to US military police even though the American perpetrators were off-duty and the British victims had no connection to the armed forces. They were tried in US courts martial on American bases. Tyrion Davis allegedly raped two women in Suffolk. He was convicted of one charge of sexual assault, but cleared of 10 further counts of sexual assault and abusive sexual contact. Hannes Marschalek allegedly exposed himself to a 16-year-old girl and four young women in Littleport, Cambridgeshire. He negotiated a plea bargain at a court martial and admitted a charge of indecent conduct. He won an appeal in a US military court that quashed his conviction on technical grounds. This ruling is now being challenged. The US has more than 12,000 US military personnel in the UK, stationed in at least 15 bases and facilities. The two biggest bases are at Lakenheath and Mildenhall, in Suffolk. Significant numbers of American military personnel live in East Anglia. One of the issues the two prime ministers discussed was the war in Ukraine, a country bordering Poland which Warsaw supports diplomatically and militarily against Russia. "We will support all efforts aimed at achieving peace," Modi said during the joint press briefing. Previous reports indicated India had formulated a plan to halt strikes on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine and protect ships transporting grain and fuel. Before traveling to New Delhi, Tusk had also indicated that India "could play a constructive role" regarding the war, saying that this aspect was "very important" to him. While no concrete steps were announced during his trip, many in Europe still hope India can use its friendship with Russia to boost peace talks. Analysts warn, however, that New Delhi's access to the Kremlin does not automatically grant it sway over Russian President Vladimir Putin and his decisions. India 'cannot guarantee peace' India is unlikely to sacrifice its own interests at Europe's insistence, says India's former ambassador to Poland Anil Wadhwa. So far, New Delhi has maintained its political and defense relationship with Moscow while calling for dialogue and diplomacy and resisting pressure to align fully with Western sanctions. Moreover, while New Delhi may be able to communicate with both Moscow and Kyiv, there is no guarantee either side will respond to its efforts or make concessions. "Poland wants India to use its access to Vladimir Putin to encourage a ceasefire and meaningful negotiations, while recognizing the limits of New Delhi's influence over Russian military decisions," he told DW. The challenge, Wadhwa said, was to translate India's diplomatic access into practical outcomes without expecting too much. "India can contribute to de-escalation and help create conditions for negotiations, but it cannot guarantee peace," he said. Europe moves closer to India despite Russia row The Polish initiative also reflects a wider European effort to deepen relations with India. Ummu Salma Bava, chairperson and Jean Monnet Chair at the Centre for European Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, told DW that Tusk's visit had two objectives: strengthening ties between India and his own country and persuading New Delhi to factor in the EU's perspective on the Ukraine war. "The Ukraine war has become central to European security. India's strong association with Moscow despite the war has raised concerns on developing cooperation on security between India and the EU," Bava said. Poland, a frontline state, does not want Russia to gain additional economic benefits from its relationship with India. So far, according to Bava, "both sides have managed to compartmentalize the Ukraine issue" while advancing cooperation on trade, security and defense. But their differences could complicate future efforts to expand defense and security cooperation, she warned. US shift on Ukraine lets EU allies change stance Ajay Bisaria, another former envoy to Poland, says India's position has "matured into that of a potential peacemaker" and its ability to communicate with both Kyiv and Moscow is now perceived as useful. According to Bisaria, not even Warsaw regards "the Russia question" as a "significant irritant in the India-Europe or India-Poland relationship." "Europe, and Poland in particular, understands the depth of India's partnership with Russia, just as India appreciates the very different lens through which much of Europe views Moscow and the war in Ukraine," Bisaria told DW. https://hotnews.ro/volodimir-zelenski-af.text: Kievul speră să obțină rezultate concrete în cadrul negocierilor privind soluționarea conflictului cu Rusia în acest an, a declarat miercuri președintele ucrainean, care a precizat că multe lucruri depind de modul în care Statele Unite abordează Moscova. Zelenski a făcut aceste declarații la Dublin, într-o conferință de presă susținută alături de prim-ministrul irlandez Micheal Martin, după două zile de discuții conduse de SUA între negociatorii ucraineni și ruși, la Abu Dhabi, capitala Emiratelor Arabe Unite (EAU). „Trecem prin aceste atacuri masive. Desigur, vrem să obținem rezultate până la sfârșitul acestui an și, bineînțeles, vom face tot ce ne stă în putință pentru ca acest lucru să se întâmple”, a spus Zelenski în cadrul conferinței de presă, potrivit agenției internaționale de presă Reuters. „Multe depind în prezent de formatul dialogului de mâine (joi, n.r.) dintre părțile americană și rusă… Cred că este foarte important și pentru americani… să obțină un rezultat în acest an, în opinia mea, având în vedere ceea ce vedem că se întâmplă. Și mi se pare că ei (americanii, n.r.) își doresc cu adevărat acest lucru”, a continuat liderul ucrainean. Însă, vorbind despre garanțiile de securitate pentru Ucraina, el a sugerat că SUA ar putea forța Rusia să accepte încetarea războiului. Zelenski a adăugat că ucrainenii „au nevoie de răspunsuri foarte concrete” în această privință. „Vom vedea răspunsurile americanilor și ale rușilor. Există unele lucruri care depind de Rusia – multe lucruri depind de Rusia”, a adăugat el, citat de Sky News . „Dar mai multe depind de Statele Unite – de voința lor. Pentru că ei sunt liderii”, a punctat președintele ucrainean. Negocierile de pace de la Abu Dhabi conduse de emisarii SUA, primele care au avut loc din februarie încoace, au produs un acord privind eliberarea unui număr mare de prizonieri de război, dar au adus puține alte anunțuri concrete privind măsurile de încetare a războiului. Cei doi emisari prezidențiali americani, Steve Witkoff și Jared Kushner, urmează să se deplaseze joi la Moscova pentru discuții cu președintele rus Vladimir Putin, iar de acolo vor pleca cu un avion pentru a se întâlni cu Zelenski la Dublin. Kushner a afirmat, într-o conferință de presă susținută anterior în cursul zilei de miercuri, că nu există încredere între cele două părți , dar a descris negocierile de la Abu Dhabi drept „un prim pas bun”. Negociatorul ucrainean David Arakhamia a spus că discuțiile au fost dificile, delegația rusă sosind cu „directive stricte”, dar că acestea au creat un „impuls pozitiv” în vederea găsirii unei soluții înainte de sfârșitul anului. Negociatorul-șef al delegației ruse, Vladimir Medinski, a declarat pentru televiziunea de stat rusă că, în urma tratativelor din capitala EAU, el consideră că se apropie un acord de pace, dar a adăugat că multe depind de poziția Ucrainei și a Statelor Unite.
